Reply: We thank the reviewer for this important clarification and agree that our work does not directly model planetary magnetic field generation or quantify field strength through magnetic Reynolds numbers or interior modeling. We explicitly acknowledge that the pressure–temperature range required for stabilizing this phase likely exceeds those of Uranus and Neptune. Therefore, any connection to planetary magnetic fields should be regarded as speculative.

The manuscript “Thermally driven superhelical state in CH compound under planetary interior conditions” written by Liu, Cohen and Sun, proposes a computational study of a system having stoichiometry CH at high pressure and high temperature conditions. This work proposes the new CH material as relevant for planetary science, particularly to understanding the properties of ice giant planets. After reading the manuscript, I could find both positive and negative points relative to the methodology and results.
I think that the authors have predicted an interesting system that could potentially manifest 1-D superionicity, and it is intriguing that a helix structure of carbon is stable above 1 TPa of pressure. However, there are two fundamental aspects of this work that made me concerned and that I will further develop with my comments: 1) The superhelical state seems to be just 1-D superionicity given by the confinement of the carbon lattice; and 2) the theoretical calculations appear to have significant limitations that should be addressed.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments. We agree that the new state is constrained by the carbon framework, within which hydrogen diffuses along quasi-one-dimensional channels. However, these channels are helical rather than linear, forcing hydrogen atoms to move in spiral trajectories. To clarify this distinction, we developed a mean-square-displacement (MSD) model capturing direction-dependent diffusion. Unlike a conventional 1D superionic state—where D = D = 0 and D > 0 (DF = 1)—the superhelical state exhibits both axial diffusion (D > 0) x y z z and angular diffusivity of 5.50 s−1, yielding an effective DF = 2. The MSD shows plateaus of ∼0.34 ˚A2 in x and y (total 2R2 ), characteristic of rotationally mobile hydrogen as in two dimen- H sionalplastic-crystalphasesinxy plane. Toaddresstheoreticallimitations, weconductedextensive validation, including convergence of k-mesh, cutoff energy, and exchange–correlation functionals; system-size and convex-hull tests; and an explicit treatment of the C 1s core. These extensive validation tests provide strong confidence in the reliability and robustness of our results.

This made it difficult to understand the goodness of some of the parameters the authors chose. A structure should, even if theoretical, should always be provided to guarantee and help reproducibility.

- The authors study a system starting from very high pressure, from 1 TPa to 3 TPa. At such pressures it is not possible to trust the core potentials, even if modified as the authors do in some cases. The 1s orbital of carbon will affect the intraatomic 2s and the interactions with the other carbon atoms. Therefore, all electrons calculations should be performed.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for raising the concern regarding core-electron ionization. Previous studiesbyBethkenhagenet al. (Phys.Rev.Research2020)andCl´erouinet al. (Phys.Rev.E2022) explored the equivalence between pressure- and structure-defined ionization in hot dense carbon. These works demonstrated that 1s ionization in carbon occurs only at much higher pressures (P∼ 237.6 TPa) and temperatures (T ∼ 100 eV) than those investigated in the present study. Moreover, we also performed band-structure calculations using the CP2K code, which can explicitly include all-electron effects, including the carbon 1s orbital. The resulting band structure is nearly identical to that obtained without accounting for the 1s orbital (Fig. R10). Relative to diamond carbon and Cs-IV hydrogen, the CH compound has a formation energy of 21 meV per atom at 1000 GPa, consistent with our FP-LAPW result (Fig. S21 in Supplemental Materials). Therefore, we confirm that the 1s electrons remain tightly bound and are not stripped in our simulations. The electronic structure and bonding characteristics are thus governed entirely by valence electrons, and no core ionization effects are expected to influence our results.

Reply: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the issue regarding the spiky density of states (DOS). Upon checking, we found that the spiky DOS was caused by using a small smearing width of 0.02 eV, which is indeed too low for metallic CH. We have now employed a more appropriate smearing parameter of σ = 0.2 eV, resulting in a smooth DOS (Fig. R11). We also performed detailed convergence tests for the VASP calculations by varying the k-mesh (Fig. R12) and energy cutoff (Fig. R13). The total energy differences are below 1 meV between k-meshes of 0.025×2π and 0.015×2π, and between cutoff energies of 1500 eV and 2000 eV. Furthermore, the corresponding band structures remain essentially unchanged under these variations. Therefore, we conclude that a cutoff energy of 1500 eV and a k-mesh of 0.025×2π are sufficient to ensure well-converged results for our calculations. For the QE convergence test, we varied both the plane-wave cutoff energy and the kmesh to assess the internal energy of the CH compound (Fig. R14). Our calculations converged with a cutoff energy of 100 Ry and a 16×16×16 k-mesh.

- I question the interpretation that “Thus, the new state can be characterized by a combination of superionic behaviors in the z direction and plastic behaviors in the xy plane of H atomic motion, finally inducing helix H chain rotation along the z-axis in the rigid C framework. Reply: We thank the reviewer for this careful and insightful analysis. We agree that the newly identified state is confined by the carbon framework, within which hydrogen diffuses along quasi-one-dimensional channels. These channels, however, are not strictly linear but follow a helical geometry, causing the hydrogen atoms to move along spiral trajectories. To elucidate this unique diffusion behavior, we have developed a mean-square-displacement (MSD) model (Method section) that captures this direction-dependent motion. This model clarifies the distinction between the observed behavior and that of a conventional one-dimensional (1D) superionic state. In a typical 1D superionic phase, hydrogen diffusion is confined to a single direction (taken here as the z-axis), where D = D = 0 and D > 0, yielding a diffusional dimensionality of DF = 1. In contrast, x y z in our identified state, hydrogen exhibits not only significant diffusion along z (D > 0) but also z substantial angular diffusivity of 5.50 s−1, resulting in an effective diffusional dimensionality of DF = 2. The key signature of the new motion behaviour appears in the MSD: both the x and y components saturate at plateau values of approximately 0.34 ˚A2 each (summing to 0.68 ˚A2, which equals 2R2). This plateau behavior is characteristic of plastic crystal phases, similar to H those observed in high-pressure simulations of ammonia. Although solid phases also display MSD plateaus, their amplitudes are typically much smaller than 2R2. We fully agree with the reviewer that this new state corresponds to a form of confined superionicity, in which hydrogen diffusion is restricted by the geometry of the underlying scaffold—in our case, the helical carbon framework that guides hydrogen motion along helical pathways. In the manuscript entitled ’hermally driven superhelical state in CH compound under planetary interior conditions’, the authors report the results of their numerical study of the CH compounds in the multi-megabar regime. They have performed a series of ab initio calculations using DFT to examine possible stable compounds of CH at 0K, their stability based on a phonon spectrum analysis,andtheirpropertiesatfinitetemperature. Basedontheirstudy,theauthorsconcludethat CH forms a stable double-helix in the multimegabar regime. At low temperature, the compound is stable, but above 1000 K, it becomes “superhelical” with hydrogen diffusing along the channel formed by the carbon chain. At about 4000 K, the system becomes superionic, and ultimately melts at about 6000K. This specific geometry imprints on the transport properties, both ionic and electronic. Theauthorsthenconsiderpossibleconsequencesforplanetaryinteriorssuchasicegiant planets, and their magnetic field.
The topic is of interest for multiple communities since it brings novel structure and concept for planetary physicists, but also high pressure scientists, and the warm dense matter community in general. However, the conclusion of superionicity/superlicity is in stark contrast with what experimentalists have observed with the clear formation of diamond and a phase separation of carbon and hydrogen in the megabar regime. It is quite easy to misinterpret superionicity in DFT-MD when it is actually a demixing process that should occur, since the finite-size effects tend to overstabilize the superionic structure. There are also a few shortcomings in the interpretation of the results (see details below). For all these reasons I do not believe this work can be published. I append below detailed comments to justify this recommendation and to help strengthening this work.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and critical assessment of our work. We fully acknowledge the experimental evidence showing that C–H systems tend to dissociate into diamond and hydrogen in the megabar regime. Our own static calculations also confirm that no C–H compound remains stable between 500 and 1000 GPa. We removed the isochores below 1000 GPa from the phase diagram to avoid potential misunderstandings. However, existing experiments are currently limited to pressures up to ∼300 GPa, whereas the new CH compound we report emerges above 1000 GPa—conditions that have not yet been experimentally accessible. Our study, therefore, aims to extend the theoretical understanding of C–H chemistry into this ultra-high-pressure regime, complementing rather than contradicting current experimental observations. To ensure that the predicted superhelical behavior is not an artifact of finite-size effects or simulation details, we performed additional defect-stability tests, large-scale molecular dynamics, and two-phase coexistence simulations. All these independent checks consistently demonstrate that the superhelical and superionic phases persist above 1000 GPa, supporting their intrinsic thermodynamic stability in this previously unexplored pressure–temperature range.
Detailed comments: - numerous experimental studies led by Dominik Kraus’ team have shown that almost any CxHy plastics dissociate into diamond and phase separated hydrogen in the megabar regime. The conclusion from the authors regarding the superionicity of the system is thus questionable. Indeed, it is possible that finite-size effects overstabilize the homogeneous system. I would recommend to perform a few additional tests to ensure the reality of this system. The first one would be the most robust but also the most expensive. I would suggest to perform a careful thermodynamic integration to compare the homogeneous superionic system with the dissociated one. If this is too intricate to perform, it would be interesting to use the largest cell and introduce a defect with one carbon and one hydrogen removed to see if the cell remains stable. An alternative would be to start from a liquid simulation and cool it down slowly to see if a superionic phase appears. Without such a study, it is not possible to entirely justify that the superionic phase is stable, in my opinion.

Following the reviewer’s recommendations, we performed several additional tests to confirm the robustness of the predicted superionic CH phase. First, we constructed a 3×3×3 supercell (324 atoms) and introduced a vacancy by removing one carbon and one hydrogen atom (Fig. R19). DFT-MD simulations indicate that the CH compound remains in a superhelical state at 2000 K, with the carbon framework preserved and hydrogen continuing its helical diffusion within the channels. A small number of hydrogen atoms near the vacancy can spill into the cavity created by the missing carbon, but their motion remains locally confined rather than freely diffusive. At 4000 K, the CH compound remains in a superhelical state but exhibits stronger vibrations. The hydrogen atoms begin to move freely throughout the lattice at 5000 K, marking the onset of the superionic state. These simulations demonstrate that the CH compound retains both the structural integrity of the carbonframeworkandthecharacteristichydrogendiffusionbehavioreveninthepresenceofapoint defect, highlighting the intrinsic robustness of the superhelical phase.

Due to the limited accessible box size (324 atoms) and simulation time (12 ps) in FPMD, we further trained a machine-learning potential (MLP) for the CH compound using the DeepMD framework implemented in the LAMMPS package. The training dataset consists of DFT-MD trajectories spanning 500–3000 GPa and sampling all relevant states—solid, superhelical, superionic, and liquid. The final root-mean-square errors (RMSE, Fig. R20) are 0.008 eV/atom for energies and 0.477 eV/˚Afor forces, enabling large-scale MD simulations. Hydrogen diffusivity converges for system sizes above 1500 atoms with only minor fluctuations. Additionally, radial distribution functions (RDFs; Fig. R21c,d) for C–C, C–H, and H–H pairs show excellent agreement between MLP-MD (scatter) and DFT-MD (lines) for both superhelical and superionic trajectories, confirming the reliability of the MLP-MD simulations with 1500-atom supercells. At 4000 K, the hydrogen can diffuse freely in the xy plane and jump from one channel to another. These long-time, large-cell MLP-MD simulations demonstrate that both the superhelical and superionic states are intrinsically stable at 1000 GPa. Movies of the defect-containing superhelical and superionic trajectories have been included in the Supplementary Information.

Reply: We thank the referee for the careful evaluation of our manuscript and for the positive assessmentofourresponsestothemethodologicalandcomputationalcomments. Below,werespond in detail to the remaining points regarding the interpretation and discussion of the results.
(1) The choice of the superhelical state terminology is likely to become misleading. I have read the previous comment by the author, and I still believe that the confined superionicity in a 1-D channel, and the fact that this channel has the structure of a helix, are two different things. The helical motif is structural, while the different melting temperature between carbon and hydrogen is the phase transition to superionic. If the carbon motif was different, like a large nanotube, that would probably change the transition temperature, but the two systems (nanotube and helix) would still be two pseudo 1-D superionic systems. In fact, the plateau in x and y described by the authors might still be obtained in motifs that are not helical. Therefore, I remark that the two aspects, carbon motif and type of superionic transition, are different, and that mixing them in one term – superhelix – would not have any real meaning. I understand the intention to find a term to describe the 1-D superionicity – 2-D plasticity, or pseudo 1-D superionicity. However, that should probably not be related to the motif.

We also appreciate the referee’s candid assessment concerning physical realizability, planetary relevance, and experimental feasibility.
We fully agree that the super-helical phase is stabilized only at ultra-high pressures (>1 TPa) andthatbelowthisregimeC–Hmixturesdissociateintoelementalcarbonandhydrogen, consistent withbothourcalculationsandexistingexperimentalevidence. Wefurtheragreethatsuchpressure– temperatureconditionsareunlikelytobebroadlyrealizedinplanetaryinteriors,andthatlarge-scale convection, compositional stratification, and thermal effects would strongly limit the persistence of mixed C–H phases. Likewise, we acknowledge that experimental realization would be extremely challenging and, at present, speculative.
However, we respectfully disagree with the implication that these constraints diminish the scientificsignificanceoftheworkatthelevelrequiredforNature Communications. Thecentralcontri- 7 bution of this manuscript is not the prediction of a practically realizable planetary or experimental phase, but rather the identification of a previously unrecognized transition mechanism—the quasi- 1Dsuperionicstate—thatprovidesaconceptualbridgebetweenconventionalplasticandsuperionic matter under extreme confinement.
Specifically, this work demonstrates that helical confinement can give rise to a distinct intermediate regime characterized by coupled structural order and ionic mobility, that superionic behavior can emerge through a topologically constrained pathway rather than simple sublattice melting, and that bonding, transport, and diffusion can become strongly anisotropic and decoupled in light-element systems under extreme compression. These insights are general and transferable, extending beyond the specific C–H system studied here, and are relevant to a broad community spanning condensed-matter physics, high-pressure chemistry, and materials science.
In response to the referee’s concerns, we have substantially revised the manuscript to make this distinction explicit in 4th paragraph of page 6. The revised version removes claims of direct planetaryornear-termexperimentalrelevance, clearlypresentsthequasi-1Dsuperionicphaseasan extreme-condition limiting case, and foregrounds the transition mechanism and transport physics as the primary contribution, with realizability discussed only as contextual motivation.
Regarding journal scope, while we respect the referee’s recommendation for a more specialized venue, we believe that the revised manuscript now clearly articulates a broad conceptual advance aligned with the mission of Nature Communications: to publish work that introduces new physical mechanisms of general interest, even when realized under extreme or currently inaccessible conditions.
We are grateful for the referee’s forthright and insightful comments, which have helped us sharpen both the framing and the scientific message of the work, and we believe the revised manuscript now addresses these concerns directly.

While we agree that sub-percent-level variations in PDF peak amplitudes should not be over-interpreted, the improved agreement with DFT confirms that the main conclusions of this work are robust.
